question: Describe a time you worked with others to reach a shared goal.
answer_a: I worked on the returns desk at a furniture shop with three others, and in the January sale we had a target of clearing every return within two days. My supervisor put it to the team as, Emily will run the paperwork because she knows the forms, and the rest of you move the stock, so my role was clear from the start. I kept a list of each day's returns on the desk and went through it with the others every morning so they knew which pieces were coming back. When one of the porters hurt his wrist and we started to fall behind, I asked the Saturday staff if two of them could come in for an extra morning, and both did. We cleared the backlog that week and met the two day target for the rest of the sale.

question: Tell me about a time you solved a difficult problem at work.
answer_a: I ran the repairs counter at a phone and laptop shop. One month we had a run of laptops coming back within a week of a screen repair with the same flickering fault, and a regular customer came in and said, Oluwaseun, this is the second time. I pulled the job sheets for every returned repair and found they had all been fitted with screens from one delivery. I tried two unused screens from that box on a bench machine and both flickered, so the cause was a bad batch and not our fitting. For that reason I stopped using the box, refitted the returned laptops with screens from a different delivery and sent the faulty batch back to the supplier. None of the refitted laptops came back.

question: Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict in a team.
answer_a: I was a charge hand on a road resurfacing crew, and two of the lads had fallen out over who drove the roller and who was left raking by hand. I had meant to just set a rota myself, but that evening I talked it over with my wife, who said I ought to ask them first, so the next morning I asked each of them what the problem was. One told me his worry was his back, which was why he wanted the roller, and he had not wanted to say so in front of the others. I changed what I was going to do. Instead of a straight rota I put him on the roller for the heavy days and took a turn on the rake myself so the other lad was not carrying it all. I told the foreman the pair of them had sorted the pattern out between them. The sniping stopped and the crew got through that stretch without anyone going off sick.

question: Describe a problem where the cause was not obvious, and what you did.
answer_a: I had just come back from maternity leave to my job as a payroll officer when staff at one of our depots began reporting that their overtime was a few pounds short. It was not every person or every week. I broke the calculation into its steps, the clock data, the rate table and the rounding, and checked each one against ten payslips by hand. The clock data and the rates were right, and the difference came from the rounding, which had been changed to the nearest quarter hour while I was away. I could either change the setting back or keep it and pay a correction each month. Changing it back was quick but needed the system offline for an evening, while the monthly correction avoided that but meant extra work for me every month from then on. I chose to change it back. I checked the result by recalculating the same ten payslips and then the whole depot's next pay run by hand, and they matched.

question: Tell me about a time you solved a difficult problem at work.
answer_a: I am fifty eight and I work on the customer service desk at a bus company. Last winter we had a jump in complaints that the first bus on one route was leaving the terminus early. I went through the complaint forms, which all named the same stop, and then compared the printed timetable at that stop with the driver's running card. The stop still showed the old time, four minutes later than the one the drivers had been working to since the autumn change, so the bus was on time and the sign was wrong. As the cause was the sign and not the driver, I asked the depot to replace the timetable case at that stop and put a notice on the route page in the meantime. The complaints about that bus stopped within a fortnight.

question: Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict in a team.
answer_a: I was a ward clerk on a busy surgical ward, and the nurses and the porters were arguing most days about patients arriving late for theatre. I was about to draw up a new timetable myself, but I asked the head porter and two of the nurses for their side first. The head porter said his concern was that his team were being called for three patients at once and then blamed for the last one. So I gave up on the timetable and instead started phoning the porters' desk the evening before with the next day's order, and I asked the nurses to tell me by seven if it changed. When one of the nurses was off, I covered the calls for that bay as well. I made sure the ward sister knew the evening call had been the head porter's suggestion. In my review my manager wrote that Priya had got two teams talking again and that she had done it without being asked, which was kind, but what mattered to me was that patients stopped being late for theatre and the arguments stopped.

question: Tell me about a time you solved a difficult problem at work.
answer_a: I was a technician at a tyre and exhaust centre, and a customer came back twice saying her grey estate car still pulled to the left after we had serviced it. I tested the possible causes one at a time: first the tyre pressures, then the wheel alignment, then I swapped the front tyres over, and after the swap it pulled to the right, so it was a faulty tyre and not the steering. I had two options. Fitting one new tyre was cheaper, but it would leave different tread depths across the axle. Fitting a pair cost about twice as much but kept the two sides the same. I recognised it was her decision, so I explained both and recommended the pair, and she agreed. Afterwards I checked it on a straight, level stretch of the dual carriageway with my hands light on the wheel, then drove back past the petrol station, and the car tracked straight the whole way.

question: Describe a problem where the cause was not obvious, and what you did.
answer_a: I worked in a bakery on the early shift, and for two weeks the bread from the second oven was coming out pale and heavy. Nobody knew the reason. I wrote down the oven temperature every thirty minutes for three days and I asked the night baker what had changed. The numbers showed that the oven lost heat every time the big mixer was running, and the night baker told me that an electrician had moved the mixer onto the same circuit as the oven. So the cause was that the two machines were sharing the power. Because of this, I changed the timetable so that we mixed the dough before the oven was switched on, and I asked the owner to call the electrician back. From the next day the bread from the second oven came out the right colour and weight.

question: Tell me about a time you solved a difficult problem at work.
answer_a: I was a maintenance fitter at a bottling plant and one filling line kept stopping with a jam about once an hour. I tested the likely causes one at a time: first the bottle guides, then the conveyor speed, then the capping head, and the jams only stopped when I slowed the capping head by hand. A worn clutch in the capping head was letting it run fast. I could replace the clutch that night, which meant four hours with the line down, or fit a spare head from stores in forty minutes and repair the worn one on the bench later. I chose the spare head because it cost far less running time, though it left us without a spare for a few days. To check it I stood at the line for the next two hours and counted no jams, and I looked at the stoppage log at the end of the week, which showed none on that line.
